questions.stem: Which prediction follows deductively from cell theory when an organism is newly discovered?

options.text: The organism consists of one or more cells
options.why: Cell theory applies to living organisms, so it predicts cellular organization before the new organism is examined.

options.text: The organism consists entirely of eukaryotic cells
options.why: Cell theory predicts cells, but it doesn't predict their type. The organism could be prokaryotic.

options.text: Every cell in the organism contains one nucleus
options.why: Prokaryotes lack nuclei, and several eukaryotic cell types have many nuclei or none.

options.text: Every cell in the organism performs photosynthesis
options.why: Photosynthesis belongs to certain cells and organisms. It isn't part of cell theory.

questions.stem: A cell is 25 µm long, while its micrograph is 50 mm long. What is the magnification?

options.why: This comes from dividing 50 by 25 before matching the units. The image length is given in millimeters.
This is ten times too small. Converting 50 mm gives 50,000 µm.
Convert 50 mm to 50,000 µm, then divide image size by actual size: 50,000 ÷ 25 = 2000.
The measurements have been multiplied rather than divided. Magnification is image size divided by actual size.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes resolution from magnification?

options.text: Resolution separates nearby points; magnification enlarges the image
options.why: Resolution determines whether fine detail can be distinguished. Magnification only describes how large the image is compared with the specimen.

options.text: Resolution enlarges organelles; magnification increases image contrast
options.why: Magnification enlarges the image, while contrast concerns differences between light and dark regions. Neither definition given here describes resolution.

options.text: Resolution measures specimen size; magnification measures field diameter
options.why: Specimen size and field diameter are measurements used in microscopy. They aren't the definitions of resolution and magnification.

options.text: Resolution stains specimens; magnification focuses the objective lens
options.why: Staining and focusing are preparation and microscope-use techniques. They don't define either quantity.

questions.stem: What makes immunofluorescence useful for locating a particular protein in a cell?

options.text: Fluorescent antibodies bind specifically to the target antigen
options.why: Antibody specificity connects the fluorescent signal to a particular antigen, usually the protein being located.

options.text: Electrons cause every membrane in the specimen to fluoresce
options.why: Immunofluorescence is a light-microscopy method. Its selectivity comes from antibodies, not electron illumination.

options.text: A stain colors every organelle according to its natural pigment
options.why: Most organelles lack diagnostic natural pigments. Labeling every structure would also remove the method's specificity.

options.text: Freezing separates the two layers of each target protein
options.why: Freezing and splitting a specimen describes freeze fracture. It isn't how antibodies locate a protein.

questions.stem: Which combination identifies a typical prokaryotic cell?

options.text: Nucleoid DNA, 70S ribosomes and no membrane-bound nucleus
options.why: A prokaryote keeps its DNA in a nucleoid region, uses 70S ribosomes and lacks a membrane-bound nucleus.

options.text: Nuclear chromosomes, 80S ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum
options.why: A nucleus, cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes and rough ER are features of eukaryotic cells.

options.text: Nucleoid DNA, 80S ribosomes and a double nuclear membrane
options.why: A nucleoid and a nuclear membrane can't describe the same typical cell. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S.

options.text: Circular DNA, lysosomes and membrane-bound mitochondria
options.why: Lysosomes and mitochondria are membrane-bound eukaryotic organelles. Prokaryotes lack both.

questions.stem: Which organelle modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles?

options.text: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
options.why: Rough ER synthesizes proteins on attached ribosomes and begins their transport. Later sorting and packaging occur in the Golgi apparatus.

options.text: Golgi apparatus
options.why: The Golgi apparatus receives cell products, modifies and sorts them, then packages them into vesicles.

options.text: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
options.why: Smooth ER is associated with lipid synthesis and other metabolic processes. It lacks attached ribosomes.

options.text: Lysosome
options.why: A lysosome contains hydrolytic enzymes used in intracellular digestion. It doesn't run the cell's packaging pathway.

questions.stem: A micrograph shows a cell wall, a large sap vacuole and no visible chloroplasts. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: It can't be a plant cell because chloroplasts are absent
options.why: Many plant cells, including root cells, don't contain chloroplasts. Chloroplast absence doesn't exclude a plant cell.

options.text: It is definitely fungal because all fungi have large sap vacuoles
options.why: Fungal cells can have vacuoles, but a large sap vacuole doesn't prove fungal identity. Wall composition would matter.

options.text: It may be a non-photosynthetic plant cell
options.why: A cell wall and large sap vacuole support plant identity, while a non-photosynthetic plant cell may lack chloroplasts.

options.text: It must be animal because chloroplasts are absent
options.why: Animal cells lack cell walls and don't have a large permanent sap vacuole. Chloroplast absence alone isn't enough.

questions.stem: Which feature makes a mature mammalian red blood cell atypical among eukaryotic cells?

options.text: It contains many nuclei formed by cell fusion
options.why: That describes a skeletal muscle fiber. A mature mammalian red blood cell loses its nucleus.

options.text: It has naked circular DNA in a nucleoid
options.why: That describes prokaryotic genetic organization. A mature mammalian red blood cell has no nucleoid.

options.text: It lacks a nucleus after differentiation
options.why: The nucleus is lost as the mammalian red blood cell matures, making it an anucleate eukaryotic cell.

options.text: It shares one cytoplasm with neighboring cells
options.why: Continuous multinucleate cytoplasm describes an aseptate fungal hypha, not separate red blood cells.

questions.stem: Which observation best supports the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria?

options.text: They contain hydrolytic enzymes inside a single membrane
options.why: That describes lysosomes. Hydrolytic enzymes don't provide the required prokaryote-like evidence.

options.text: They contain 70S ribosomes and naked circular DNA
options.why: These resemble prokaryotic ribosomes and DNA, supporting the origin of mitochondria from an engulfed prokaryote.

options.text: They are assembled by the Golgi apparatus from vesicles
options.why: Golgi vesicles don't assemble mitochondria. Mitochondria grow and replicate within cells.

options.text: They contain 80S ribosomes enclosed by a nucleus
options.why: Cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes and a nucleus are eukaryotic features. Mitochondria contain 70S ribosomes and no nucleus.

questions.stem: Why can two differentiated cells have different structures even when they contain the same genome?

options.text: They express different genes and produce different proteins
options.why: Different patterns of gene expression change which proteins are produced, leading to specialized structures and functions.

options.text: They replace their DNA with genes taken from nearby tissues
options.why: Differentiation doesn't normally replace the genome. Cells alter which existing genes they express.

options.text: They translate every gene but destroy different chromosomes afterward
options.why: Cells don't normally express every gene or discard chromosomes to specialize. Regulation occurs at gene expression.

options.text: They receive different ribosome types during each cell division
options.why: Different cytoplasmic ribosome types don't explain specialization. The important difference is which genes are expressed.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches an atypical cell structure with its number of nuclei?

options.text: Skeletal muscle fiber: no nuclei
options.why: Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleate because precursor cells fuse during their development.

options.text: Aseptate fungal hypha: many nuclei
options.why: An aseptate hypha has continuous cytoplasm containing many nuclei without complete cross-walls separating them.

options.text: Mature sieve tube element: one nucleus
options.why: A mature sieve tube element lacks a nucleus and depends on an associated companion cell.

options.text: Mature mammalian red blood cell: many nuclei
options.why: A mature mammalian red blood cell has no nucleus. It doesn't become multinucleate.

questions.stem: What is one advantage of multicellularity identified in A2.2?

options.text: Every cell can perform every function independently
options.why: That describes the demand placed on a unicellular organism. Multicellular organisms can divide functions among specialized cells.

options.text: All cells can lose their plasma membranes
options.why: Cells still need plasma membranes to maintain boundaries and regulate exchange. Multicellularity doesn't remove that requirement.

options.text: Specialized cells can divide biological functions
options.why: Cell specialization permits division of labor, and cooperation among those cells can support a larger body.

options.text: The organism no longer needs gene expression
options.why: Gene expression is required for cell function and differentiation. Multicellularity makes its regulation especially important.
